findings.title: [P1] Non-finite and non-integer values bypass validation and are returned as timeouts
findings.body: The new guard `if (timeout <= 0)` cannot reject `NaN` because every comparison with `NaN` is `false`. So `parseTimeout("abc")` — or any non-numeric string such as `"10ms"` — now returns `NaN` instead of throwing `"invalid timeout"`. Likewise `parseTimeout("Infinity")` and `parseTimeout("1e309")` return `Infinity` (positive infinity is `> 0`), `parseTimeout(".5")` returns a fractional `0.5`, and `"9007199254740993"` returns an integer outside the safe range. All of these inputs were rejected before this PR: the old `Number.isSafeInteger(parseInt(value, 10))` check threw for `NaN`, `Infinity`, fractions, and unsafe integers. The function's error contract — reject invalid configuration with `"invalid timeout"` — is therefore broken for any malformed input, which is exactly the realistic failure mode (typos, unit suffixes like `"10s"`, exponent overflow). Downstream, `NaN`/`Infinity` delays are coerced by Node timers to ~1 ms, so any future timeout/cancellation consumer would fire immediately rather than surface the misconfiguration. Restore a finite, safe-integer (and ideally integer) check before returning.

findings.title: [P2] `Number()` changes parsing semantics from base-10 integer prefix to full-string numeric conversion
findings.body: Even for inputs that remain accepted, returned values change: `"1e3"` previously returned `1` (`parseInt` stops at `e`) and now returns `1000`; `"0x10"` previously threw (`parseInt(..., 10)` yields `0` → `timeout <= 0`) and now returns `16` (hex interpretation); `"1.5"` previously returned the truncated `1` and now returns `1.5`. These contradict the PR's stated intent of "preserving existing contracts" and can silently change effective timeout durations by orders of magnitude. If stricter full-string parsing is the goal, make it explicit with `Number.parseInt` + safe-integer validation, or document the accepted grammar.
